drapeaux.note: Langue du texte fourni : français ; auteur d'origine : Antonio di Tuccio Manetti (Vie de Brunelleschi, en italien). Les deux expressions entre guillemets (« aussi petit qu'une lentille », « de la taille d'une pièce de monnaie ») sont retraduites depuis le français.

accroche: Around 1415, a Florentine architect drills a hole in a painting and holds up a mirror. What he lets us see exists in no painting before him.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the early 15th century, the Florentine architect Filippo Brunelleschi paints a small panel showing the Florence Baptistery, seen from inside the neighboring cathedral, then unfinished. Nothing in the subject distinguishes this painting from any other city view. The apparatus Brunelleschi builds around it, however, has no known equivalent before that date.

The most detailed account of this experiment comes from a biography of Brunelleschi written in the 1480s by an admiring younger contemporary, Antonio di Tuccio Manetti, who claims to have held the panel in his hands and examined it several times.

## Looking Through a Hole to See a Mirror

At the center of the panel there is a small hole, drilled from the painted side, about as wide as a lentil. On the back, the opening widens like a pyramid to the size of a coin. Manetti describes the procedure precisely: the viewer places an eye against the hole, on the unpainted side, and with the other hand holds a mirror up facing the painting. What he sees then is the reflection of the painting, not the painting itself. The part of the panel showing the sky was covered with a thin sheet of polished silver, which reflects the real sky and its moving clouds, blurring the boundary between the painted image and the real scene even further.

The effect, according to Manetti, was striking: seeing the reflection in the mirror, you believed you were looking at the real thing. What Brunelleschi works out with this device is a single vanishing point, toward which all the parallel lines of a scene observed from a fixed position converge. The mathematical principle was known to Greek and Roman geometers, but lost to Western painting throughout the Middle Ages.

The exact date of the experiment is still debated among art historians: the Encyclopædia Britannica places it around 1410-1415, while others propose different dates, from 1401 to 1425. The original panel has not survived.

## From a Private Experiment to a Public Rule

Brunelleschi publishes nothing: his demonstration remains an apparatus to be shown, not a treatise to be read. It is the architect and humanist Leon Battista Alberti who, in 1435, sets down the rules of linear perspective in writing for the first time, in his treatise *Della pittura*, which he explicitly dedicates to Brunelleschi. The dedication directly acknowledges a debt.

What perspective changes is not just the appearance of paintings. Before Brunelleschi, the size of a painted figure could signal its importance rather than its actual distance: a king larger than his subjects, a saint larger than the faithful. Once linear perspective is codified, Western painting adopts a system in which distance alone governs apparent size, whatever the importance of the subject depicted. A mirror held up in front of a hole, one day in early 15th-century Florence, ended up redefining what a painting is supposed to show: no longer a hierarchy, but a point of view.

repere.texte: The hole drilled on the painted side is described by the biographer Manetti as “as small as a lentil”; the flared opening on the eye side, “the size of a coin.” The original panel has not survived, but Manetti claims to have held it in his hands and examined it several times.
repere.source: Antonio di Tuccio Manetti, Life of Brunelleschi (c. 1480), cited by webexhibits.org

carte.punch: A hole in a painting, a mirror held up in front: that is how Western perspective is born.
carte.idee: Around 1415, Brunelleschi paints the Florence Baptistery on a panel with a hole drilled in it, to be viewed as a reflection in a mirror. The experiment demonstrates the principle of the single vanishing point, the foundation of linear perspective in Western painting.

quiz.question: What exactly does Brunelleschi's panel-and-mirror experiment demonstrate?
choix: That oil paint, still rare in Florence at that date, renders light far better than the tempera used until then
That the Florence Baptistery had been poorly proportioned by the Romanesque architects who built it three centuries earlier
That a polished, well-oriented mirror can replace a painted panel in the interior decoration of a religious building
That a scene viewed from a fixed point can be rebuilt on a flat surface through lines converging on a single vanishing point
quiz.explication: The apparatus brings out the principle of the single vanishing point: the parallel lines of a scene viewed from a fixed point converge on one and the same point on the painted surface. It is neither a comparison of painting techniques, nor a judgment on the Baptistery, nor a decorative use of the mirror, which serves here only as a verification tool.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the viewer look at Brunelleschi's painted panel, according to the procedure described by Manetti?
choix: He places his eye against a hole drilled on the painted side and holds a mirror up facing the painting with his other hand
He observes the panel from a distance, without any special device, from the Baptistery's forecourt
He looks at the panel through a magnifying lens fixed on a stand
He observes only the panel's reflection in the water of a basin
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Manetti describes the procedure precisely: the viewer places his eye against the hole drilled on the painted side, and with the other hand holds a mirror up facing the painting. What he sees then is the reflection of the painting in the mirror, not the painting itself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What covers the sky portion of the panel, and what effect does it produce?
choix: A thin sheet of polished silver, which reflects the real sky and its moving clouds
A layer of dark blue paint, to heighten the contrast with the rest of the panel
A plate of tinted glass, which gives an effect of artificial depth
Nothing in particular: the sky is painted like the rest of the picture
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The part of the panel showing the sky was covered with a thin sheet of polished silver, which reflects the real sky and its moving clouds, blurring the boundary between the painted image and the real scene a little further still.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who first sets down the rules of linear perspective in writing, and in what year?
choix: Leon Battista Alberti, in 1435, in Della pittura
Filippo Brunelleschi himself, in 1415, in a treatise that remained in manuscript
Antonio di Tuccio Manetti, in his biography of the 1480s
Andreas Werckmeister, in 1425, in an architecture treatise
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Brunelleschi publishes nothing; his demonstration remains an apparatus to be shown. It is Leon Battista Alberti who, in 1435, sets down the rules of linear perspective in writing for the first time, in his treatise Della pittura, which he explicitly dedicates to Brunelleschi.
